prize_parts.citation: For the conception and leadership of the ATLAS and CMS experiments, which led to the experimental discovery of the Higgs boson

statement.case_for: After the full exchange I keep the Higgs experimental discovery as my preferred configuration, with the same three names. Nothing said in round 1 disputes the science: a predicted particle was found independently by two experiments and then characterised through its couplings and quantum numbers, and the 2013 prize recognised only the theory. The discovery sits squarely at the centre, which is the order in which I think the committee should work: identify the discovery first, then the people behind it. The credit problem is real, but it is a problem of drafting and not of science. A citation built on the conception and long-term leadership of the two detector programmes gives a principled boundary, namely the founders and not the spokespersons of a given year, and it can be defended as such. I have not moved my lead, but I have moved my confidence: I now think the committee will probably prefer a more compact credit.
statement.case_against: The attribution weakness is the one raised by Mehlig, Pearce, Johansson and Kroll, and I cannot dismiss it. Two collaborations of thousands cannot be represented by three names without excluding someone with a serious claim, and Gianotti, who led ATLAS at the announcement, is the most obvious omission. My founder-based boundary is a judgement and not something the evidence forces. Circuit QED and optical lattice clocks have cleaner credit and broader support, and I accept that either would be a sound prize. The discovery-versus-invention distinction I leaned on does not by itself outweigh a cleaner attribution if the committee finds the Higgs credit cannot be settled.

responses.point: Pearce now leads with circuit QED, reports that the Higgs is his seventh choice because three names cannot fairly represent two collaborations, and earlier proposed Gianotti, Jenni and Virdee.
responses.response: I agree that the collaboration question cannot be set aside and that this is the real obstacle. Where I differ is that I think it argues for a deliberate rule and not for demotion. If the citation is tied to the conception and leadership of the detectors, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee follow from that rule, whereas Gianotti follows from a rule based on the moment of announcement. I would accept the second rule only if the committee prefers it, and I concede that a Gianotti, Jenni, Virdee trio is no less defensible than mine. I also thank him for accepting my point on IceCube, whose source identifications remain thin.

responses.point: Johansson argues that circuit QED is a defined discovery with a defined date, distinct from the 2025 tunnelling work, and that the Higgs is overdue in a way circuit QED is not, while the four-name credit is his difficulty.
responses.response: His distinction between macroscopic quantum behaviour and coherent single-photon exchange with an engineered atom is a fair one, and I withdraw the implication that circuit QED is merely the same community honoured twice. I still read it as closer to an architecture than a finding about nature, so I do not rank it first, but I now regard it as a strong alternative. I thank him for conceding the urgency of the Higgs. His point about the four names is the one I cannot answer except through the founders rule, and I accept that this is a judgement and not a proof.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice clock is a distinct step beyond the 2005 comb and the 2012 ion prize, that the Nobel Prize does not wait for a standards body, and that the citation should be worded around the lattice scheme and its accuracy.
responses.response: I accept the distinction. A many-atom ensemble held with the light shift cancelled is a new idea and not a better comb or a better ion, and I withdraw the lineage objection as a bar. I also accept that redefinition of the second is not a condition. My remaining reservation is narrower: the payoff so far is accuracy and stability, and the discovery content, such as a new test of constants or a measured redshift at small scales, is still arriving. If the committee prefers a mature, cleanly credited prize with Katori and Ye, I would support it. The citation would need to keep to the lattice scheme, as he proposes.

responses.point: Mehlig places the Higgs second and says the science is not the issue but the evidence does not settle whether the founders, Gianotti, or spokespersons at the announcement should be credited, so he would not force the choice.
responses.response: This is the most accurate statement of the difficulty, and I agree that the evidence does not settle it. I would not ask the committee to force it on thin grounds, but I think it must be settled one way or the other, since declining to decide leaves the experimental Higgs unrecognised indefinitely. I take his narrow-citation point for circuit QED as sensible, with strong coupling and dispersive readout kept as the credited discovery and Girvin and Huang acknowledged as outside the trio.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks lattice clocks first as a separate physical idea from the comb, judges the atomic physics directly, and finds my eighth rank for circuit QED too low if it rests only on the 2025 prize.
responses.response: Her reading of the atomic physics is more authoritative than mine, and her argument that the lattice scheme solves a problem no comb advance addressed is persuasive. On circuit QED, my low rank rested on the architecture-versus-discovery question and on the 2025 adjacency, and the replies from Johansson, Mehlig and Pearce have weakened the adjacency part. I would no longer place it eighth. I would put both circuit QED and lattice clocks ahead of the alternatives I have not named.

uncertainties: Whether three names can be defended from four candidates and two collaborations of thousands, and whether the founders rule or the spokesperson rule is the better principle.
Whether the committee prefers a compact, mature and cleanly credited prize (circuit QED or lattice clocks) to the experimental Higgs discovery, given that credit for the Higgs is the main obstacle.
Whether circuit QED, now that Johansson, Mehlig and Pearce have separated it from the 2025 tunnelling work, is better described as a discovery or as an enabling architecture.
Whether the decisive discovery payoff of lattice clocks has yet arrived, and how the 2005 and 2012 prizes affect the reading of the lineage.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict has changed since round 1. My documented connections (Gross, Rubinstein, Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group) do not touch any shortlisted candidate or credited name. Johansson and Lindroth have disclosed proximity to circuit QED, and I note this without adjusting my own position.
